title: What happens during a complete shower replacement and waterproofing rebuild?
summary: A complete shower replacement may involve more than changing the tray and enclosure. The work can include opening up the old installation, checking the walls and floor, rebuilding unsuitable areas, planning the pipework and waste, and preparing a waterproof system before the finished surfaces go back.
author: Nigel Harvey
author_note: Nigel carries out domestic plumbing and bathroom work in Guildford and surrounding Surrey areas. The Merrow ensuite project linked below records a complete refurbishment he carried out, including the preparation behind the finished surfaces.

sections.heading: When a shower needs more than a new enclosure
paragraphs: A leaking shower, loose tiles or a moving tray can make a simple replacement look attractive. But a new enclosure cannot put right a weak base, an unsuitable wall build-up or a leaking waste hidden underneath. The first question is what is failing and how far the affected construction extends.

Not every shower needs a full rebuild. If the supporting structure, waterproofing and connections are sound, a smaller repair or replacement may be possible. The scope should follow an inspection, with hidden conditions explained when they become visible.

sections.heading: What should be checked before ordering fittings?
paragraphs: Measure the finished opening as well as the old tray. Tiles and wall finishes reduce the space available, and enclosure adjustment ranges vary by model. Check the proposed tray shape, door opening, access and the manufacturer’s dimensions together.

The water supply and waste arrangement matter too. A shower valve must suit the actual hot and cold supplies and operating conditions. The waste route, available fall, trap position and future access need checking before committing to the tray height or layout. A photograph cannot establish all of these details.

sections.heading: Opening up the old installation
paragraphs: Once the relevant supplies are safely isolated, the old fittings and affected finishes can be removed to reveal the construction. This allows the installer to inspect the tray support, wall framing or masonry, board condition and accessible pipework.

Visible damp or dark marking is a reason to investigate, but appearance alone does not prove a particular leak or condensation cause. Damaged materials, drying needs and ventilation should be assessed before the area is closed again. A persistent moisture or structural problem may need specialist input.

sections.heading: Rebuilding the support and planning access
paragraphs: The tray needs the support specified by its manufacturer. Walls also need a sound substrate suitable for the chosen boards, tiles and fittings. Any repair or reconstruction should be agreed before finishes conceal it.

A heavy glass enclosure needs a fixing arrangement appropriate to its weight and the actual wall construction. Tile and a lightweight board do not, by themselves, establish that a fixing is suitable. The installer should check the enclosure instructions, suitable support and where fixings and penetrations will go. Access to serviceable fittings should be planned rather than discovered after tiling.

sections.heading: Waterproofing is a system, not just a board
paragraphs: A waterproof board can be part of the solution, but the installation also has joints, corners, fixings, pipe penetrations and a junction with the tray. Those details need the treatment specified for the selected system. Products should be compatible and installed to their current instructions.

For example, Marmox describes Multiboard as having a waterproof core and provides joint-sealing products. That does not mean every board joint or connection becomes waterproof without the specified treatment. Do not assume that the same detailing applies to another board or tray.

Tiles, grout and a visible bead of sealant should not be relied on as the entire waterproofing design. The underlying system and the tray junction must be considered before the final finish. Curing and drying times depend on the actual adhesive, grout and sealant products and site conditions.

sections.heading: Plumbing, tiling and the final checks
paragraphs: Supply connections, valve compatibility and the waste should be checked while they remain accessible. Once the tray, waterproofing and tiled surfaces are ready, the enclosure and fittings can be installed and sealed according to their instructions.

Allow the specified curing time before using the shower. The final checks should include operation of the shower, drainage and accessible connections, with attention to leakage and the enclosure seals. A successful initial check does not remove the need to maintain seals, keep the waste clear and investigate future changes.

sections.heading: A real example: the Merrow ensuite
paragraphs: In Nigel’s published Merrow, Guildford ensuite project, strip-out revealed problems with the existing wall and insulation build-up, including visible mould in affected areas. Nigel stripped back the affected construction and rebuilt the wall build-up, rather than covering it with a new finish.

The recorded work included Marmox waterproof building boards, sealing and waterproofing at joints and vulnerable areas, plumbing, the shower tray and fittings, WC, basin and vanity, heated towel rail, tiling and flooring. The case study shows the preparation and finished room in nine genuine photographs. It does not claim a definitive mould cause or specialist mould remediation.

sections.heading: What should a quotation explain?
paragraphs: Ask what is included in strip-out and disposal, supporting construction, waterproofing, plumbing, tray and enclosure fitting, tiling and making good. Clarify which fittings you are supplying and whether the quoted scope assumes the existing walls and floor are sound.

Hidden damage can change the work. Agree how findings and additional costs will be discussed before extra work proceeds. The duration depends on the extent of the rebuild, access, drying and product curing requirements; one project’s timescale is not a reliable promise for another.

safety: This guide explains the considerations for planning work; it is not a step-by-step installation instruction. Do not remove fittings or open construction just to provide photographs.

Stop using a shower if a leak may be reaching electrics. Keep clear of wet electrical equipment and obtain appropriate professional help. Electrical shower work and bathroom electrical alterations need a competent electrician and any applicable certification.

Gas appliances, gas pipework and boiler gas work require an appropriately qualified Gas Safe registered engineer. Nigel Harvey Plumbing does not claim Gas Safe, WaterSafe or WIAPS registration. Unvented hot-water safety controls and discharge pipework need a suitably competent specialist; do not bypass or adjust them.

faqs.question: Can I just replace the silicone?
faqs.answer: A failed visible seal may be repairable, but new silicone will not correct a moving tray, a leaking waste or damaged construction. The cause needs checking before deciding that resealing is enough.

faqs.question: Do all shower replacements need new walls?
faqs.answer: No. Reuse depends on the condition and suitability of the supporting construction and waterproofing. The inspection determines what needs repair or replacement.

faqs.question: Should I order the enclosure before a visit?
faqs.answer: It is safer to confirm the finished opening, tray compatibility and adjustment range first. Send the proposed product details so the dimensions and installation requirements can be checked.
